summary: The France Excellence Eiffel scholarship is a French government award for international master's and PhD students. It pays a monthly allowance (from January 2026: €1,200 for master's, €2,100 for doctorate) plus return flights, insurance, housing help and cultural activities, but not tuition. You cannot apply alone: a French university or grande école must choose you from its own applicants and nominate you to Campus France, so winners are top students with a clear academic and career project.
lookfor: Excellence of your academic record (many schools ask for strong grades over your last three years)
A coherent study and career project linking your past studies, the French programme and your future

Fit with the priority fields: biology and health, ecological transition, mathematics and digital, engineering sciences, law and political science, economics and management, French history/language/civilisation
Your home institution's own ranking of you against other applicants (it only forwards its best files)
For PhD: the quality of the research project and supervision arrangement
cycle: The 2027 call is not yet published on Campus France. Last round: call opened 1 Oct 2025, French institutions submitted by 8 Jan 2026, results from 30 Mar 2026. Schools are already running the 2027–28 round (e.g. Bordeaux INP's internal deadline is 20 Nov 2026), so expect internal deadlines from late October to late November and a national deadline in early January—check your target school's Eiffel page now.

eligibility.q: Are you a foreign national (not French, not a dual French national)?
eligibility.no: French nationals cannot receive Eiffel; look at French domestic grants instead.

eligibility.q: Are you within the age limit: for master's, 29 or younger (last round: born after 31 March 1996); for PhD, 35 or younger?
eligibility.no: Age limits are strict. Check the current call when it opens; if you are over, look at French embassy grants or university-specific awards.

eligibility.q: Have you never been put forward for Eiffel before, and are you not already on a French government scholarship?
eligibility.no: Several schools exclude earlier Eiffel applicants and current French government grantees; check your school's rules.

eligibility.q: Are you applying for a master's or PhD at a French institution that takes part in Eiffel, starting in autumn 2027?
eligibility.no: You must first apply for admission to a French programme; the school then nominates you.

eligibility.q: Is your intended field one of the Eiffel priority areas?
eligibility.no: Other fields are not funded by Eiffel; consider French embassy scholarships or the school's own awards.

eligibility.q: Can you pay tuition (low at public universities, higher at grandes écoles and private schools)?
eligibility.no: Eiffel does not cover tuition; choose a public university or a school that waives fees for Eiffel scholars.

steps.title: Understand how Eiffel really works
steps.why: Many applicants wait for a student portal that does not exist; only French institutions can submit Eiffel files.
do: Read the Campus France Eiffel page for students: funding, fields, durations.
Note: you apply to a French programme AND ask that school to consider you for Eiffel.
Write down that the school, not Campus France, sets your real (earlier) deadline.
tips: Think of Eiffel as two competitions: first inside the school, then nationally.
avoid: Emailing Campus France to 'apply'—they only accept files from institutions.
check: I can explain the nomination process in one sentence.

steps.title: Shortlist 2–3 French programmes that nominate for Eiffel
steps.why: Your nominating school decides whether your file ever reaches Campus France.
do: Search for English- or French-taught master's (M1 or M2) or PhD positions in a priority field.
On each school's site, search 'Eiffel' to find its internal procedure, contact and internal deadline.
Note each school's tuition (Eiffel does not pay it) and admission deadline.
For PhD: identify a French supervisor and confirm they will support an Eiffel nomination.
tips: Sorbonne University, Bordeaux INP and UTBM publish clear Eiffel procedures—use them as models of what schools ask.
Some schools set a grade floor: Bordeaux INP only forwards files averaging at least 15/20; Sorbonne asks for 15/20 over the last three years. Ask how your grades convert.
avoid: Choosing a school that does not take part in Eiffel.
check: For each school I know its internal Eiffel deadline and contact.

steps.title: Build your timeline from the school's internal deadline
steps.why: Last year internal deadlines fell between late October and late November—months before the national 8 January date.
do: List each school's admission deadline and internal Eiffel deadline.
Set your own target two weeks earlier than the earliest one.
Schedule: transcripts by week 2, CV and project by week 4, references by week 5.
tips: Some schools have two phases (e.g. a short pre-file in October, the full form in November).
avoid: Working to the Campus France date instead of the school's date.
check: My calendar shows the earliest internal deadline in red.

steps.title: Apply for admission to the French programme
steps.why: Schools usually nominate only candidates they want to admit; your admission file is the base of your Eiffel file.
do: Use each school's admission portal (or the Études en France procedure if your country uses it—check with Campus France in your country).
Upload transcripts, CV, motivation letter and references as required.
Tick or request Eiffel consideration as the school instructs (some ask you to email a named Eiffel contact).
tips: Nigerian applicants: Campus France has an office in Nigeria; ask them whether your programme uses Études en France.
avoid: Applying to the programme but forgetting the separate Eiffel request.
check: My admission application is submitted and I have asked for Eiffel consideration.

links.t: Campus France Eiffel programme for students

steps.title: Gather transcripts, diplomas and ID
steps.why: Schools commonly ask for transcripts from your last three years and all diplomas since secondary school.
do: Request official transcripts for at least your last three years of higher education.
Scan all diplomas (and class ranking if available) from secondary school onwards (e.g. WAEC, degree certificate).
Scan your passport photo page; check it is valid for the full study period.
Translate any document not in English or French if your school requires it.
tips: Ask for a letter of class rank—schools like seeing you are at the top of your cohort.
avoid: Sending a passport that expires during your studies.
check: All diplomas, transcripts and ID are scanned as clear PDFs.

steps.title: Get language proof
steps.why: Programmes taught in French need a French certificate; English-taught programmes may want IELTS/TOEFL.
do: Check your programme's language of instruction and required level.
For French-taught: book DELF/DALF or TCF at an Alliance Française.
For English-taught: check if an English-medium degree letter is accepted; otherwise book IELTS/TOEFL.
Upload the certificate with your admission file.
tips: Even for English-taught degrees, basic French (A1/A2) on your CV shows commitment to living in France.
avoid: Applying to a French-taught programme without the required French level.
check: I have the certificate or confirmation my school needs.

steps.title: Write a 1–2 page CV
steps.why: Schools ask for a short CV (often max two pages) as part of the Eiffel form.
do: Lead with education: degree, institution, grades, rank.
Add research projects, internships, work (NYSC if relevant), awards, languages.
Keep it to two pages and use a clean European-style layout.
tips: Show links to the priority field (e.g. environment projects for 'ecological transition').
check: It is two pages or less and error-free.

steps.title: Write your study and professional project
steps.why: The 'projet professionnel' (1–2 pages at many schools) is how selectors judge the coherence of your plan.
do: Check your school's form for the exact title and length (often 1–2 pages).
Explain where you are now: degree, results and key experience.
Explain why this French programme: courses, labs, internships, French expertise in your field.
Explain your career plan after the degree and its benefit for your country or sector.
Show the logic: past → French programme → future.
tips: Selectors value a clear, realistic link to your home country's needs or to France–home cooperation.
avoid: Writing a general essay on 'my passion' with no plan.
Copying the same letter for every school.
check: A reader could draw my path in three boxes from this letter.

steps.prompt: Professional and study project: why this programme in France and how it fits your career plan.

steps.title: PhD only: prepare the research project
steps.why: For doctoral nominations, the research project and supervision are central.
do: Agree a topic with your French supervisor (and home supervisor if co-supervised).
Write: background, objectives, methods, timeline, expected results, and why France.
Ask your doctoral school head how to access the online Eiffel form.
tips: Check the current call for how long doctoral funding lasts and whether time in France must be split into periods.
avoid: Contacting the doctoral school after its internal deadline.
check: My supervisor has approved the project text.
steps.prompt: Doctoral research project with supervision arrangements.

steps.title: Ask for recommendation letters
steps.time: ask 3–4 weeks before the internal deadline
steps.why: Many schools make letters optional, but a strong letter helps your school rank you first.
do: Ask one or two lecturers (or employer) who know your work well.
Send them your CV, project text, programme name and the school's deadline.
Ask for a signed letter on letterhead, in English or French.
tips: Ask the referee to mention your rank in class if they can.
avoid: Generic letters that do not name the French programme.
check: I have signed letters or confirmation they will be sent.

steps.title: Submit the Eiffel file to your school
steps.why: Only the school's best files are forwarded to Campus France.
do: Fill in the school's Eiffel application form (or online access given to you).
Attach CV, project, transcripts, diplomas, ID, language proof and letters.
Proofread every page.
Submit before the internal deadline and keep the confirmation email.
tips: Ask the school's Eiffel contact to confirm your file is complete.
avoid: Sending documents to a programme director when the school says to send them to a central Eiffel contact.
check: I have written confirmation the school received my Eiffel file.

steps.title: Wait for the school's choice and the national result
steps.why: Schools rank and forward files by early January; Campus France publishes results from about the end of March.
do: Expect the school's internal decision in December/January.
Check the Campus France Eiffel page from late March for the results list.
Meanwhile, keep your admission offer active and apply for other funding as a backup.
tips: Respond quickly if your school asks for missing documents in December.
avoid: Turning down your admission offer while waiting.
check: I know when and where results will be published.

steps.title: If selected: visa, bank account and arrival
steps.why: Campus France pays the allowance monthly into a French bank account and arranges travel and insurance.
do: Follow Campus France's instructions for the scholarship acceptance and flight booking.
Apply for your long-stay student visa at the French consulate/visa centre with your award letter.
On arrival, open a French bank account and send your registration certificate to Campus France.
Plan housing early; you may be eligible for housing help.
tips: Eiffel cannot be combined with other French government, Erasmus+ or AUF funding at many schools—check before accepting another award.
avoid: Missing classes or exams; attendance is an obligation of the award.

faq.q: Can I apply for Eiffel directly?
faq.a: No. Only French higher education institutions submit Eiffel applications. You apply to a programme and ask the school to nominate you.
No. It pays a monthly allowance, flights, insurance, housing help and cultural activities. Choose a school with low or waived fees.
Last round: 29 for master's (born after 31 March 1996) and 35 for PhD. Check the 2027 call when published.
No. That is the date for institutions. Your school's internal deadline is usually in October or November.
Up to 12 months for M2, up to 24 months for M1, up to 36 months for an engineering degree.
